IndyGuitarist Wampler Pedals browse by type distortion/fuzz/overdrive distortion browse by enclosure pedal Wampler Pedals PlexTortion Published on November 2, 2007 Wampler Pedals distortion pedal Information Wampler Pedals The Plextortion is a distortion pedal that was originally designed to emulate a JCM800 with celestion greenbacks (Back in Black era AC/DC tones through van halen, dokken, ratt, and all those amazing 80's rock "cranked Marshall" tones). It has a very 'brown' sounding distortion, a bit similar to the pinnacle pedal. It differs from the pinnacle in that it is a tighter distortion, more like preamp tube distortion where the pinnacle is a bit looser, more like power tube distortion. The Super Plextortion differs from the standard Plextortion in that it has 3 totally different gain structures. It is more of a transparent type of tone (more of a celestion vintage 30 type of tone) where the standard plextortion has more of a mid focused marshally 'greenback' sound to it. Basically, the super plextortion is more of a modern sounding distortion where the standard plextortion is more vintage sounding. I've noticed that some guys like play their distortion pedals that emulate marshall tones THROUGH a marshall. Let's be honest - I can play a chorus pedal through a marshall and get a very "marshally" sounding chorus pedal... In my opinion this isn't a fair or accurate representation of a pedal. Because of this, I record my clips and videos through everyday affordable guitars and amps in order to be as accurate as possible. sources.excerpt: Wampler Pedals Super Plextortion and Pinnacle Review: Dual High-Gain Powerhouses Tested Side-by-Side | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / gear reviews gear reviews Wampler Pedals Super Plextortion and Pinnacle Review: Dual High-Gain Powerhouses Tested Side-by-Side By Nina Harper July 10, 2026 Introduction: Two Distinct Paths to High-Gain Tone Wampler Pedals’ Super Plextortion and Pinnacle represent two philosophically divergent approaches to high-gain overdrive within the same product family. The Super Plextortion ($279 USD) is a meticulously voiced recreation of the legendary Plexi-era Marshall tones — specifically targeting the saturated midrange growl of a cranked ’68 Marshall Super Lead 100W head through a 4x12 cabinet loaded with Celestion G12M ‘Greenbacks’. The Pinnacle ($299 USD), by contrast, is a modern high-headroom distortion designed for tight low-end response, articulate note separation, and dynamic sensitivity — engineered to complement high-gain metal and progressive rock rigs without sacrificing touch responsiveness. Both are true-bypass, analog circuits housed in CNC-machined aluminum enclosures measuring 4.75" × 3.75" × 2.0", weighing 1.2 lbs each, and powered by standard 9V DC (center-negative) with a current draw of 22mA (Super Plextortion) and 24mA (Pinnacle). Over six weeks of daily testing across three guitar/amp combinations — a 1963 Fender Stratocaster into a 1978 Marshall JCM800 2203, a 2015 Gibson Les Paul Standard through a Friedman BE-100, and a PRS SE Custom 24 into a Fender Twin Reverb — these pedals revealed nuanced differences in harmonic complexity, compression behavior, and pedalboard integration. Circuit Architecture & Design Philosophy Under the hood, both pedals employ discrete transistor-based gain stages rather than op-amp ICs, preserving organic clipping characteristics and minimizing phase inversion artifacts. The Super Plextortion uses a three-stage JFET-driven topology inspired by the cascading preamp section of a non-master-volume Marshall. Its first stage features a dual-ganged J201 JFET configured for soft asymmetrical clipping; the second stage adds a 2N5457 JFET with adjustable bias via the ‘Tone’ pot; and the third stage employs a matched pair of 2N5459s for output saturation. This architecture deliberately emulates the voltage sag and natural compression of tube-driven signal paths — a key reason why it responds so authentically to guitar volume roll-off (tested from 10 to 3.5 on a 500kΩ CTS pot). Super Plextortion: The Analog Emulation Approach The Super Plextortion’s signal path includes a passive tone stack derived directly from Marshall’s original Baxandall-style EQ network, implemented with 1% metal-film resistors and polypropylene film capacitors (including a 0.022µF Orange Drop coupling cap between stages). Its ‘Gain’ control sweeps from clean boost (at 1–2 o’clock) through classic Plexi crunch (3–5) to full-blown lead saturation (7–10). Crucially, the ‘Volume’ knob is post-clipping but pre-EQ, meaning tone shaping remains consistent regardless of output level — a design choice that preserves midrange focus even at unity gain settings. Pinnacle: The Modern High-Fidelity Engine The Pinnacle departs significantly from vintage emulation. Its four-stage gain structure combines JFETs and silicon diodes in a hybrid clipping configuration: Stages one and two use matched 2SK372 JFETs for low-noise pre-saturation; stage three introduces symmetrical silicon clipping (1N4148 diodes) for aggressive harmonics; and stage four utilizes a proprietary buffered output stage with active EQ feedback. Unlike most high-gain pedals, the Pinnacle’s ‘Drive’ control doesn’t simply increase gain — it dynamically adjusts clipping threshold *and* low-end tightness via an internal 18V virtual rail circuit (achievable with the included Wampler Triple Tap power supply or any isolated 18V DC source).
